<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_1>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> What do a salary raise every year and the rungs of a ladder have in common — and why does that pattern matter? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_1:two_sequences>> Picture Reena. She lands her first job at 8 000 rupees a month, and every single year her salary climbs by exactly 500 rupees. <<TRACE:salary-row>> <<FOCUS:salary-jumps>> Watch the jumps between each year — 500, 500, 500, 500. Every gap is identical. <<POINT:salary-jumps>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now compare that to a savings scheme where your money grows to five-fourths of itself every three years — 8 000, then 10 000, then 12 500, then 15 625. <<TRACE:savings-row>> <<FOCUS:savings-jumps>> Look at those gaps — 2 000, then 2 500, then 3 125. The jumps keep changing. This is NOT the same kind of pattern. <<POINT:savings-jumps>> <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the big question: what is the one thing that makes Reena's salary sequence special — and the savings sequence NOT special in the same way? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:constant-jump-highlight>> It's this — in Reena's sequence, the jump from one term to the next is always exactly the same. That constant, equal step is what defines an Arithmetic Progression. <<PAUSE:short>> We give that fixed, equal jump a name: the common difference. In Reena's case the common difference is 500. <<POINT:salary-jumps>> <<PAUSE:short>> A ladder whose rungs shorten by 2 cm each step? Arithmetic Progression — common difference of negative 2. A sequence that multiplies or grows unevenly? Not an AP. <<POINT:savings-jumps>> <<FOCUS:constant-jump-highlight>> So the one thing to brand into your brain: an Arithmetic Progression is any sequence where the gap between consecutive terms is always the same — that gap is the common difference. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_2>>
What if I told you that with just TWO numbers, you can predict the millionth term of an infinite list — without writing out a single number in between? <<FOCUS:number-line-axis>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_2:ap_number_line>> Here is a number line. Watch what happens when I place dots at 1, 4, 7, 10, 13. <<TRACE:number-line-axis>> <<FOCUS:jump-arrow-1>> Each dot lands exactly 3 steps to the right of the one before — the gap is always the same. <<TRACE:jump-arrow-1>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-1>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-1>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> That fixed jump — 3 in this case — is called the common difference, d. Every term is just the term before it plus d. <<POINT:jump-arrow-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> A list that behaves this way — same fixed jump between every pair of neighbours — is called an Arithmetic Progression, or AP. And d does not have to be positive. If I subtract 30 each time — like 100, 70, 40, 10 — d is negative 30. If every term is the same number, d is zero. Still an AP. <<POINT:term-dot-1>> <<FOCUS:term-dot-5>> Here is the real question: if I asked you for the 100th term of 1, 4, 7, 10 … without listing all 100 — how would you find it? <<PAUSE:long>> Look at the dots again. To reach the 2nd dot you made 1 jump. The 3rd dot took 2 jumps. The 5th took 4 jumps. The nth dot always takes exactly n minus one jumps of size d from the start. <<TRACE:jump-arrow-3>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-3>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-3>> <<TRACE:jump-arrow-3>> Each jump adds d once. By the time you reach the nth dot, you have made exactly n minus one jumps from the start — so the nth term is the first term, plus that many jumps of size d. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a_n = a + (n-1)d|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:nth-term-label>> Each jump adds d once. By the time you reach the nth dot, you have made exactly n minus one jumps from the start — so the nth term is the first term, plus that many jumps of size d. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:nth-term-label>> So the formula is: a-n equals a plus n minus one times d. For the 100th term of our sequence: 1 plus 99 times 3 — that is 298. No listing needed. <<POINT:nth-term-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> Those two numbers — a, the first term, and d, the common difference — completely describe the entire infinite list. That is the power of an AP. <<POINT:term-dot-1>> <<POINT:term-dot-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_4>>
<<FOCUS:forward-row>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_4:gauss_trick>> A ten-year-old boy once added every whole number from 1 to 100 in his head — in seconds. No calculator, no adding one-by-one. His name was Gauss, and the trick he used is what we're learning today. Gauss wrote the sum forwards: 1 plus 2 plus 3, all the way to 100. <<TRACE:forward-row>> Then he wrote the exact same sum backwards underneath: 100 plus 99 plus 98, all the way down to 1. <<TRACE:backward-row>> <<FOCUS:pair-brace-first>> Here's the magic — what do you get when you add the very first column? One plus one hundred. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:pair-brace-last>> One hundred and one! And the last column? One hundred plus one — again one hundred and one. Every single pair adds up to the same number — first plus last always gives 101. <<TRACE:pair-brace-last>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:two-s-label>> So together, both rows equal 100 lots of 101. That's 2S — twice the sum we want. <<FOCUS:result-label>> Halve it, and S equals five thousand and fifty. Gauss nailed it. The key was pairing first and last to get the same total every time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_4:general_ap_sum>> Now let's use this exact same trick for ANY arithmetic progression — not just 1 to 100. <<TRACE:ap-forward-row>> Write the AP forwards: a, then a plus d, then a plus 2d, all the way to the last term l. Then write it backwards right underneath. <<TRACE:ap-backward-row>> <<FOCUS:ap-pair-brace>> Add each column — a plus l, then (a+d) plus (l−d) — the d's cancel and every pair gives exactly a plus l. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ap-two-s-label>> There are n such pairs, so 2S equals n times (a plus l). The sum of any AP is just n over 2 times first plus last. There are n identical pairs each summing to a plus l, so twice the sum is n times (a plus l) — halve it and you have the sum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:last-term-substitution>> But what if you don't know the last term? No problem — substitute l equals a plus (n−1)d, and the formula becomes S equals n over 2 times the bracket 2a plus (n−1)d. <<PAUSE:short>> Replace the last term l with a plus (n−1)d, since that's what the last term of any AP equals, and simplify. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S = \frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a + (n-1)d\bigr)|id=eq-2|boxed>> So which formula do you reach for? If you know the last term, use n over 2 times (a plus l). If you only know a, n, and d, use n over 2 times (2a plus (n−1)d). Same idea, two faces. <<POINT:last-term-substitution>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_5>>
<<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> What do the numbers 3, 7, 11, 15 have in common with the way a staircase is built, the way a savings account grows by the same amount every month, and the seats in a stadium row? They all follow one secret rule — and once you see it, you can't unsee it. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_5:ap_number_line>> The rule is this: start anywhere, then keep adding the exact same number every single time. That fixed jump is called the common difference, d. Look — here's our AP laid out on a line. <<TRACE:term-a>> <<FOCUS:jump-d-arrow>> Every gap between neighbours is exactly d — not approximately, not sometimes. Always d. <<TRACE:jump-d-arrow>> Here's how you CHECK whether any list is an AP: subtract each term from the next one. If every single difference comes out equal, it's an AP. If even one gap is different, it's not. <<POINT:jump-d-arrow>> <<FOCUS:term-nth>> Now, the big question — if I give you any term number n, say the 50th term, how do you find its value WITHOUT writing out all 50 terms? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Look at the number line. To get from the first term to the nth term, you make exactly (n−1) jumps of size d. So the nth term is just a plus (n−1) times d. Start at a, add d exactly (n−1) times — that's it. <<TRACE:term-nth>> <<PAUSE:short>> To reach the nth term, you make exactly (n−1) equal jumps of size d from the start — so the nth term is a plus (n−1) times d. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a_n = a + (n-1)d|id=eq-1|boxed>> So if a sequence starts at 3 and has common difference 4, the 50th term is 3 plus 49 times 4 — that's 199. No listing, no counting. One formula. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sum-bracket>> Now for the sum — what if you want to add up all the terms from the first to the nth? There's a gorgeous shortcut hiding in the picture. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Pair up the first term and the last term — their average is the middle value of the whole sequence. Multiply that average by n, and you've added them all up. The sum equals n divided by 2, times the first term plus the last term. <<TRACE:sum-bracket>> <<PAUSE:short>> The sum of all n terms equals the average of the first and last term, multiplied by the number of terms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)|id=eq-2|boxed>> If you don't know the last term, just substitute a + (n−1)d for it, and the formula becomes n over 2 times the quantity 2a plus (n−1)d. Same idea, different packaging. When the last term isn't given, replace it with a plus (n−1)d to get the sum purely from a, d, and n. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S_n = \frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a + (n-1)d\bigr)|id=eq-3|boxed>> There's one more elegant fact worth knowing: if three numbers a, b, c are in AP, then b is exactly halfway between a and c — it equals (a + c) divided by 2. That's called the arithmetic mean, and it's the same as saying the gaps are equal. <<POINT:term-a-plus-d>> So here's what you carry out of this chapter: one — the nth term is a plus (n−1)d, start at a and add d exactly (n−1) times. Two — the sum of n terms is n over 2 times first plus last. Everything else in this topic is a consequence of those two ideas. <<POINT:term-nth>> <<PAUSE:short>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: The chapter opens by revealing that many real-world phenomena — salaries, staircase steps, stadium seating — follow a hidden numerical rhythm. It then formalizes this rhythm as an arithmetic progression, equips students with the general term formula to find any term instantly, and culminates in Gauss's elegant trick for summing a long sequence without adding every number. By the end, students see AP not as an abstract formula but as a practical tool for modeling the world.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: If you started a job earning ₹10,000 a month and got a ₹2,000 raise every year, could you figure out your salary in year 15 — or your total earnings over a decade — without listing every single year? That's exactly the kind of problem arithmetic progressions were built to solve.

coverage_checklist.description: Distinguish between sequences that are APs and those that are not, using at least one real-life and one purely numerical example.
Define common difference d and show it can be positive, negative, or zero, with a concrete example of each.
Derive or state the general term formula aₙ = a + (n−1)d and use it to find a specific term without listing all preceding terms.
Explain Gauss's pairing insight (or equivalent) as the motivation behind the sum formula Sₙ = n/2 · (2a + (n−1)d).
State and apply both forms of the sum formula: Sₙ = n/2·(2a+(n−1)d) and Sₙ = n/2·(a+l), clarifying when each form is convenient.
Connect the sum formula back to a real-life context (e.g., total salary over n years, total rungs climbed) to reinforce practical utility.
Consolidate the relationship between aₙ and Sₙ, noting that aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁, so the two formulas are not independent.
Close the loop on the opening hook: answer the salary problem explicitly using the general term and sum formulas learned in the chapter.

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We started with a simple question: can you find your salary in year 15 or your total earnings over a decade without listing every year? Now you can. An arithmetic progression is any sequence with a constant common difference d, and the general term formula aₙ = a + (n−1)d lets you jump straight to any term. When you need to add many terms together, Gauss's pairing trick gives us Sₙ = n/2·(2a+(n−1)d) — a formula that turns a tedious sum into a single calculation. These two formulas together mean that any AP, no matter how long, is completely under your control: you can find any term, any partial sum, and model any real situation where things grow or shrink by a fixed amount.

lesson_plans.title: Introduction to Arithmetic Progressions

hook.text: What do a salary raise every year and the rungs of a ladder have in common — and why does that pattern matter?

crucial_facts: A sequence where each term increases (or decreases) by the same fixed amount is called an Arithmetic Progression.
That fixed, constant jump between consecutive terms is called the common difference.

diagrams.purpose: Contrast an arithmetic (constant jump) sequence with a non-arithmetic (changing jump) sequence so students feel the difference before naming it.

Labels '+500' on each arrow between the salary boxes, highlighted in green.

choreography.narration: What do a salary raise every year and the rungs of a ladder have in common — and why does that pattern matter?
Picture Reena. She lands her first job at 8 000 rupees a month, and every single year her salary climbs by exactly 500 rupees.
Watch the jumps between each year — 500, 500, 500, 500. Every gap is identical.
Now compare that to a savings scheme where your money grows to five-fourths of itself every three years — 8 000, then 10 000, then 12 500, then 15 625.
Look at those gaps — 2 000, then 2 500, then 3 125. The jumps keep changing. This is NOT the same kind of pattern.
So here is the big question: what is the one thing that makes Reena's salary sequence special — and the savings sequence NOT special in the same way?
It's this — in Reena's sequence, the jump from one term to the next is always exactly the same. That constant, equal step is what defines an Arithmetic Progression.
We give that fixed, equal jump a name: the common difference. In Reena's case the common difference is 500.
A ladder whose rungs shorten by 2 cm each step? Arithmetic Progression — common difference of negative 2. A sequence that multiplies or grows unevenly? Not an AP.
So the one thing to brand into your brain: an Arithmetic Progression is any sequence where the gap between consecutive terms is always the same — that gap is the common difference.

crucial_facts: In an arithmetic progression, every term is obtained by adding the same fixed number — the common difference — to the term before it.
The nth term of an AP is given by a_n = a + (n−1)d, so you can find any term directly without listing them all.

choreography.narration: What if I told you that with just TWO numbers, you can predict the millionth term of an infinite list — without writing out a single number in between?
Here is a number line. Watch what happens when I place dots at 1, 4, 7, 10, 13.
Each dot lands exactly 3 steps to the right of the one before — the gap is always the same.
That fixed jump — 3 in this case — is called the common difference, d. Every term is just the term before it plus d.
A list that behaves this way — same fixed jump between every pair of neighbours — is called an Arithmetic Progression, or AP.
And d does not have to be positive. If I subtract 30 each time — like 100, 70, 40, 10 — d is negative 30. If every term is the same number, d is zero. Still an AP.
Here is the real question: if I asked you for the 100th term of 1, 4, 7, 10 … without listing all 100 — how would you find it?
Look at the dots again. To reach the 2nd dot you made 1 jump. The 3rd dot took 2 jumps. The 5th took 4 jumps. The nth dot always takes exactly n minus one jumps of size d from the start.
Each jump adds d once. By the time you reach the nth dot, you have made exactly n minus one jumps from the start — so the nth term is the first term, plus that many jumps of size d.
So the formula is: a-n equals a plus n minus one times d. For the 100th term of our sequence: 1 plus 99 times 3 — that is 298. No listing needed.
Those two numbers — a, the first term, and d, the common difference — completely describe the entire infinite list. That is the power of an AP.

equations.explanation_in_words: Each jump adds d once. By the time you reach the nth dot, you have made exactly n minus one jumps from the start — so the nth term is the first term, plus that many jumps of size d.

choreography.narration: A ten-year-old boy once added every whole number from 1 to 100 in his head — in seconds. No calculator, no adding one-by-one. His name was Gauss, and the trick he used is what we're learning today.
Gauss wrote the sum forwards: 1 plus 2 plus 3, all the way to 100.
Then he wrote the exact same sum backwards underneath: 100 plus 99 plus 98, all the way down to 1.
Here's the magic — what do you get when you add the very first column? One plus one hundred.
One hundred and one! And the last column? One hundred plus one — again one hundred and one. Every single pair adds up to the same number — first plus last always gives 101.
So together, both rows equal 100 lots of 101. That's 2S — twice the sum we want.
Halve it, and S equals five thousand and fifty. Gauss nailed it. The key was pairing first and last to get the same total every time.
Now let's use this exact same trick for ANY arithmetic progression — not just 1 to 100.
Write the AP forwards: a, then a plus d, then a plus 2d, all the way to the last term l. Then write it backwards right underneath.
Add each column — a plus l, then (a+d) plus (l−d) — the d's cancel and every pair gives exactly a plus l.
There are n such pairs, so 2S equals n times (a plus l). The sum of any AP is just n over 2 times first plus last.
But what if you don't know the last term? No problem — substitute l equals a plus (n−1)d, and the formula becomes S equals n over 2 times the bracket 2a plus (n−1)d.
So which formula do you reach for? If you know the last term, use n over 2 times (a plus l). If you only know a, n, and d, use n over 2 times (2a plus (n−1)d). Same idea, two faces.

Replace the last term l with a plus (n−1)d, since that's what the last term of any AP equals, and simplify.

Have you ever noticed how nature loves patterns? The way a sunflower arranges its petals, the perfect hexagons in a honeycomb, the spiral of a pineapple — these aren't accidents. They follow rules. And it turns out, many things in our everyday lives follow patterns too, especially patterns involving numbers. That's exactly what this chapter is about.

Now, think about a few different kinds of number patterns. Imagine someone gets a job earning eight thousand rupees a month, and every year her salary goes up by five hundred rupees. Her salary each year forms a list: eight thousand, eight thousand five hundred, nine thousand, and so on. Notice something beautiful here — each number is exactly five hundred more than the one before it. The jump is always the same.

Now compare that to a savings scheme where your money becomes one and a quarter times itself every three years. The amounts there are ten thousand, twelve thousand five hundred, fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty five — the jumps are getting bigger each time because you're multiplying, not adding.

Or think about the rabbit population example — one, one, two, three, five, eight — where each number is the sum of the two before it. That's a completely different kind of pattern.

So we have several types of patterns here, and they all behave differently. In this chapter, we're going to zoom in on just one special type: the kind where you get the next term by adding the same fixed number every single time. This is called an Arithmetic Progression. We'll learn how to find any term in such a sequence without listing all the ones before it, and how to add up a long list of such terms quickly. These skills turn out to be surprisingly useful in real life, from calculating salaries to planning savings.
examples: Think about Reena's salary. She starts at eight thousand rupees and gets five hundred more every year. So year one is eight thousand, year two is eight thousand five hundred, year three is nine thousand, and so on. The key thing to notice is that the difference between any two neighbouring terms is always exactly five hundred. It never changes. That constant difference is the heartbeat of an arithmetic progression. If you know the starting salary and that fixed jump, you can figure out her salary in any year without listing every single year in between.

Imagine a ladder where the rungs get shorter as you go up. The bottom rung is forty five centimetres long, and each rung above it is two centimetres shorter than the one below. So you get forty five, forty three, forty one, thirty nine, and so on all the way up. Again, the difference between each rung and the next is always the same — negative two centimetres. This is another arithmetic progression, just going downward instead of upward. The pattern is just as regular, just shrinking instead of growing.

Here is a fresh everyday example. Suppose you start a reading challenge. On day one you read ten pages, on day two you read fifteen pages, on day three you read twenty pages, and so on, adding five more pages every day. After a week, how many pages have you read in total? That kind of question — finding the total of a sequence where each step adds the same amount — is exactly what arithmetic progressions help us answer quickly and elegantly, without adding up every single day one by one.

Now contrast the arithmetic progression with the savings example from the textbook, where money grows to one and a quarter times itself every three years. Starting from eight thousand, you get ten thousand, then twelve thousand five hundred, then fifteen thousand six hundred and twenty five. The jumps here are two thousand, then two thousand five hundred, then three thousand one hundred and twenty five — they keep getting bigger. This is not an arithmetic progression because the difference between terms is not fixed. Spotting this difference helps you understand what makes arithmetic progressions special: that perfectly steady, unchanging step from one term to the next.

5.2 Arithmetic Progressions
Consider the following lists of numbers :
(i) 1, 2, 3, 4, . . .
(ii) 100, 70, 40, 10, . . .
(iii) –3, –2, –1, 0, . . .
(iv) 3, 3, 3, 3, . . .
(v) –1.0, –1.5, –2.0, –2.5, . . .
Each of the numbers in the list is called a term.
Given a term, can you write the next term in each of the lists above? If so, how
will you write it? Perhaps by following a pattern or rule. Let us observe and write the
rule.
In (i), each term is 1 more than the term preceding it.
In (ii), each term is 30 less than the term preceding it.
In (iii), each term is obtained by adding 1 to  the term preceding it.
In (iv), all the terms in the list are 3 , i.e., each term is obtained by adding
(or subtracting) 0 to the term preceding it.
In (v), each term is obtained by adding – 0.5 to (i.e., subtracting 0.5 from) the
term preceding it.
In all the lists above, we see that successive terms are obtained by adding a fixed
number to the preceding terms. Such list of numbers is said to form an  Arithmetic
Progression ( AP ).
So, an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term  is
obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first
term.
This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that
it can be positive, negative or zero.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, let us talk about arithmetic progressions, which is one of the most elegant and useful ideas in all of mathematics. The core idea is beautifully simple: imagine a list of numbers where you always add the same fixed amount to get from one number to the next. That fixed amount is called the common difference, and the list itself is called an arithmetic progression, or AP for short. Think about the list 1, 2, 3, 4 — you are adding 1 each time. Or the list 100, 70, 40, 10 — here you are adding negative 30 each time, which is the same as subtracting 30. Even a list like 3, 3, 3, 3 counts, because you are adding zero each time. The common difference can be positive, negative, or zero. Now, to fully describe any AP, you only need two pieces of information: the first term, which we call a, and the common difference, which we call d. Once you know those two things, you can build the entire sequence. The general form looks like this: a, then a plus d, then a plus 2 times d, then a plus 3 times d, and so on. Here is the really powerful part — we can find any term in the sequence without listing all the ones before it. The nth term equals a plus the quantity n minus 1 times d. Notice why it is n minus 1 and not n: the first term already has no d added to it, the second term has d added once, the third term has d added twice, and so the nth term has d added n minus 1 times. This formula is your shortcut to jumping straight to any position in the sequence. APs can be finite, meaning they have a last term, like the heights of students in a queue, or infinite, meaning they go on forever, like the counting numbers. To check whether a given list is an AP, just subtract each term from the one that follows it — if that difference is always the same, you have an AP.
examples: Imagine you start a savings challenge. In week one you save 50 rupees, in week two you save 100 rupees, in week three 150 rupees, and so on. Each week you save exactly 50 rupees more than the week before. This is a perfect arithmetic progression with first term 50 and common difference 50. Now, without listing all the weeks, you can find how much you save in week 20 directly: it is 50 plus 19 times 50, which equals 50 plus 950, which equals 1000 rupees. That is the power of the nth term formula.

Consider a school that gives cash prizes to class toppers. Class one gets 200 rupees, class two gets 250 rupees, class three gets 300 rupees, and this pattern continues up to class twelve. Each prize is exactly 50 rupees more than the previous one, so the common difference is 50 and the first term is 200. To find the prize for class twelve, you calculate 200 plus 11 times 50, which gives 200 plus 550, which equals 750 rupees. You did not need to list all twelve prizes — the formula took you straight there.

Here is a tricky one: the list 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 looks interesting, but is it an AP? Check the differences: 1 minus 1 is 0, then 2 minus 1 is 1, then 3 minus 2 is 1, then 5 minus 3 is 2. The differences are not the same every time, so this is not an arithmetic progression at all. This is actually the famous Fibonacci sequence, where each term is the sum of the two before it — a completely different kind of pattern. The lesson here is always check the differences before assuming something is an AP.

Think about a lift in a building that starts at the ground floor, which is floor zero, and moves up one floor every five seconds. After 5 seconds it is at floor 1, after 10 seconds at floor 2, after 15 seconds at floor 3, and so on. The floors visited form an AP with first term 0 and common difference 1. Now suppose you want to know which floor the lift reaches after 2 minutes, which is 120 seconds. That is the 24th term of the sequence, because 120 divided by 5 is 24. Using the formula, the 24th term is 0 plus 23 times 1, which is floor 23. You found the answer instantly without tracking every single floor.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, so we've been learning about arithmetic progressions — sequences where each term goes up or down by the same fixed amount. Now comes a really powerful question: what if you want to add up a whole bunch of those terms? That's what this section is all about — finding the sum of the first n terms of an AP, and doing it smartly without adding every single number one by one. The key idea here comes from a brilliant trick used by a mathematician named Gauss when he was just ten years old. He was asked to add all the whole numbers from 1 to 100. Instead of grinding through it, he noticed something beautiful. He wrote the sum forwards, then wrote it again backwards, and added the two lists together. Every pair of numbers — the first and last, the second and second-to-last — added up to 101. And there were exactly 100 such pairs. So twice the sum equals 100 times 101, which means the sum itself is 5050. Genius, right? We use exactly that same trick for any arithmetic progression. Suppose your AP starts at a, has a common difference of d, and you want the sum of the first n terms. Write the sum forwards, write it backwards, add them together. Every pair gives you two times a plus n minus 1 times d. There are n such pairs, so twice the sum equals n times that quantity. Divide by two, and you get the formula: the sum equals n over 2, times the quantity two a plus n minus 1 times d. There's also a really elegant version of this formula. Notice that two a plus n minus 1 times d is just the first term plus the last term. So the sum also equals n over 2 times the first term plus the last term. Think about that — it's like finding the average of the first and last term, then multiplying by how many terms you have. This formula is incredibly useful. If you know any three of the four quantities — the sum, the first term, the common difference, and the number of terms — you can always find the fourth. One more handy fact: if you know the sum of the first n terms and also the sum of the first n minus 1 terms, their difference gives you exactly the nth term. That's a neat connection between sums and individual terms.
examples: Think about Shakila putting money in her daughter's money box — 100 rupees on the first birthday, 150 on the second, 200 on the third, and so on, going up by 50 each time. By the 21st birthday, she's made 21 deposits. Adding them one by one would take ages. But using the formula, with first term 100, common difference 50, and n equal to 21, you get the sum equals 21 over 2 times the quantity 2 times 100 plus 20 times 50. That works out to 21 over 2 times 1200, which is 12600 rupees. The formula turns a tedious job into a few quick steps.

Imagine you're stacking logs in a triangular pile — 20 logs on the bottom row, 19 in the next, 18 in the next, and so on. You want to know how many logs are in the whole stack. The number of logs in each row forms an AP going downward. You can use the sum formula to figure out how many rows fit 200 logs total, and even how many are in the top row. This is a real-world situation where the sum formula does the heavy lifting for you.

Here's a fresh everyday example. Suppose you go for a walk every day, and on day one you walk 500 steps, on day two you walk 600 steps, on day three 700 steps, and so on — adding 100 steps each day. After 30 days, how many total steps have you taken? You have an AP with first term 500, common difference 100, and n equal to 30. The sum equals 30 over 2 times the quantity 2 times 500 plus 29 times 100. That's 15 times 3900, which equals 58500 steps in total. Without the formula, you'd have to add up 30 different numbers.

Consider the AP 24, 21, 18 and so on, where the common difference is negative 3. If you want the terms to add up to 78, you set up the sum formula and solve for n. You get a quadratic equation with two solutions — n equals 4 or n equals 13. Both are valid answers! How can that be? Well, after a while the terms become negative, so the negative terms cancel out some of the positive ones. The sum reaches 78 after just 4 terms, dips below, and then climbs back to 78 again at 13 terms. This is a beautiful reminder that when the common difference is negative, terms eventually go below zero and start pulling the sum back down.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, let's bring together everything we've learned about arithmetic progressions, because this is one of those topics that quietly shows up everywhere in mathematics and real life. An arithmetic progression, or AP for short, is simply a list of numbers where you keep adding the same fixed amount each time. That fixed amount is called the common difference, and we usually call it d. So if you start at some number a and keep adding d, you get a, then a plus d, then a plus two times d, and so on forever. That's the basic pattern at the heart of everything in this chapter. Now, how do you check whether a list of numbers is actually an AP? You subtract each term from the next one. If all those differences come out equal, congratulations — you have an AP. If even one difference is different, it's not an AP. Simple test, very powerful. The next big idea is finding any term you want without listing all the ones before it. The nth term equals a plus n minus one times d. Think about why that makes sense — to reach the nth term, you've added d exactly n minus one times to your starting value. That formula saves enormous effort. Then we have the sum formulas. To add up the first n terms, you use n over two times the quantity two a plus n minus one times d. There's also a beautiful shortcut when you know the last term — the sum is just n over two times the first term plus the last term. Imagine adding the first and last, the second and second-to-last — they all pair up to the same total. Finally, there's a lovely little bonus idea: if three numbers are in AP, the middle one is exactly the average of the other two. That middle value is called the arithmetic mean. Keep these five ideas sharp in your mind and you'll be able to handle almost any AP problem that comes your way.
examples: Think about a student saving pocket money. She saves 10 rupees in the first week, 15 in the second, 20 in the third, and so on. The common difference is 5. To find how much she saves in the 20th week, you use the nth term formula: the 20th term equals 10 plus 19 times 5, which is 10 plus 95, giving 105 rupees. No need to list all 20 weeks — one formula does the job instantly.

Imagine a cinema hall where the first row has 20 seats, the second has 22, the third has 24, and so on. This is an AP with first term 20 and common difference 2. To find the total seats in the first 15 rows, use the sum formula: 15 over 2 times the quantity two times 20 plus 14 times 2. That works out to 15 over 2 times 68, which equals 510 seats. The sum formula turns what could be a long addition into a quick calculation.

Here is the arithmetic mean idea in action. Suppose you know that three numbers are in AP and the first is 8 and the last is 20. What is the middle number? It must be the average of 8 and 20, which is 28 divided by 2, giving 14. So the three numbers are 8, 14, 20. Check it yourself — the difference between each pair is 6. The arithmetic mean is just the perfectly balanced middle value.

To check whether the list 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 is an AP, subtract each term from the next: 7 minus 3 is 4, 11 minus 7 is 4, 15 minus 11 is 4, 19 minus 15 is 4. Every difference is the same, so yes, this is an AP with common difference 4. Now try 2, 4, 8, 16 — the differences are 2, 4, 8, which are not equal, so that list is not an AP. That quick subtraction test is your first move whenever you need to identify an AP.
topics.standalone_narration_text: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> What do the numbers 3, 7, 11, 15 have in common with the way a staircase is built, the way a savings account grows by the same amount every month, and the seats in a stadium row? They all follow one secret rule — and once you see it, you can't unsee it. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:arithmetic_progressions:5_5:ap_number_line>> The rule is this: start anywhere, then keep adding the exact same number every single time. That fixed jump is called the common difference, d. Look — here's our AP laid out on a line. <<TRACE:term-a>> <<FOCUS:jump-d-arrow>> Every gap between neighbours is exactly d — not approximately, not sometimes. Always d. <<TRACE:jump-d-arrow>> Here's how you CHECK whether any list is an AP: subtract each term from the next one. If every single difference comes out equal, it's an AP. If even one gap is different, it's not. <<POINT:jump-d-arrow>> <<FOCUS:term-nth>> Now, the big question — if I give you any term number n, say the 50th term, how do you find its value WITHOUT writing out all 50 terms? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Look at the number line. To get from the first term to the nth term, you make exactly (n−1) jumps of size d. So the nth term is just a plus (n−1) times d. Start at a, add d exactly (n−1) times — that's it. <<TRACE:term-nth>> <<PAUSE:short>> To reach the nth term, you make exactly (n−1) equal jumps of size d from the start — so the nth term is a plus (n−1) times d. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a_n = a + (n-1)d|id=eq-1|boxed>> So if a sequence starts at 3 and has common difference 4, the 50th term is 3 plus 49 times 4 — that's 199. No listing, no counting. One formula. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sum-bracket>> Now for the sum — what if you want to add up all the terms from the first to the nth? There's a gorgeous shortcut hiding in the picture. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Pair up the first term and the last term — their average is the middle value of the whole sequence. Multiply that average by n, and you've added them all up. The sum equals n divided by 2, times the first term plus the last term. <<TRACE:sum-bracket>> <<PAUSE:short>> The sum of all n terms equals the average of the first and last term, multiplied by the number of terms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)|id=eq-2|boxed>> If you don't know the last term, just substitute a + (n−1)d for it, and the formula becomes n over 2 times the quantity 2a plus (n−1)d. Same idea, different packaging. When the last term isn't given, replace it with a plus (n−1)d to get the sum purely from a, d, and n. <<WRITE_EQUATION:S_n = \frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a + (n-1)d\bigr)|id=eq-3|boxed>> There's one more elegant fact worth knowing: if three numbers a, b, c are in AP, then b is exactly halfway between a and c — it equals (a + c) divided by 2. That's called the arithmetic mean, and it's the same as saying the gaps are equal. <<POINT:term-a-plus-d>> So here's what you carry out of this chapter: one — the nth term is a plus (n−1)d, start at a and add d exactly (n−1) times. Two — the sum of n terms is n over 2 times first plus last. Everything else in this topic is a consequence of those two ideas. <<POINT:term-nth>> <<PAUSE:short>>

questions.answer: First, list the pages read each day: Day 1 = 10, Day 2 = 15, Day 3 = 20, Day 4 = 25, Day 5 = 30, Day 6 = 35, Day 7 = 40. questions.q_text: A ladder has rungs that get shorter as you go up. The bottom rung is 45 centimetres long, and each rung above it is 2 centimetres shorter than the one below. What is the length of the eighth rung from the bottom?
questions.answer: The rungs form an arithmetic progression where the first term is 45 centimetres and the common difference is negative 2 centimetres. To find the eighth rung, we need to apply the fixed decrease seven times starting from the first rung. Each step up reduces the length by 2, so after seven steps the total reduction is 7 multiplied by 2, which equals 14 centimetres. The length of the eighth rung is therefore 45 minus 14, which equals 31 centimetres.

questions.q_text: A factory produces 200 units of a product in its first month. Due to efficiency improvements, it produces 15 more units every month than the month before. In which month will the factory first produce exactly 500 units?
questions.answer: We recognise this as an arithmetic progression where the first term a is 200 and the common difference d is 15. We want to find which term equals 500, so we set up the nth term formula: the nth term equals a plus the quantity n minus 1 times d. Substituting, we get 500 equals 200 plus the quantity n minus 1 times 15. Subtracting 200 from both sides gives 300 equals the quantity n minus 1 times 15. Dividing both sides by 15 gives n minus 1 equals 20. Adding 1 to both sides gives n equals 21. The factory will produce exactly 500 units in the 21st month.

options: A. Yes, because an AP must have a non-zero common difference to be meaningful.
B. Yes, because all the terms are identical, which breaks the pattern rule.
C. No, because the common difference is zero, and zero is a perfectly valid common difference for an AP.
D. No, because the sequence has exactly five terms, which automatically makes it an AP.

questions.q_text: In an arithmetic progression, the 4th term is 31 and the common difference is 6. What is the first term, and what is the 10th term?
questions.answer: We use the nth term formula: the nth term equals a plus the quantity n minus 1 times d. For the 4th term, we substitute n equals 4, the nth term equals 31, and d equals 6. This gives 31 equals a plus 3 times 6, which simplifies to 31 equals a plus 18. Subtracting 18 from both sides gives a equals 13. So the first term is 13. Now we find the 10th term by substituting n equals 10, a equals 13, and d equals 6 into the formula: the 10th term equals 13 plus 9 times 6, which equals 13 plus 54, which equals 67. The first term is 13 and the 10th term is 67.

B. Because each of the 100 numbers was paired with exactly one other number, giving 100 pairs in the doubled sum — which is why he divided by 2 at the end
C. Because 100 divided by 2 gives 50 pairs, and 50 times 101 equals 5050
D. Because the first and last terms always form 100 pairs in any sequence

questions.q_text: The sum of the first n terms of an AP can be written as n over 2 times the quantity two a plus n minus 1 times d. There is an equivalent version using the last term. Which of the following correctly explains why these two versions are equal?
options: A. Because the last term of an AP equals a plus n times d, so substituting it gives the same expression
B. Because the last term of an AP equals a plus n minus 1 times d, so two a plus n minus 1 times d is the same as the first term plus the last term
C. Because the average of the first and last term always equals the common difference

questions.q_text: Someone walks 500 steps on day one, 600 on day two, 700 on day three, and so on, adding 100 steps each day. After 30 days, what is the total number of steps taken?
The AP 24, 21, 18, ... has a common difference of negative 3. Find all values of n for which the sum of the first n terms equals 78. Explain why both answers make sense.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Write the sum formula. The sum of the first n terms equals n over 2 times the quantity 2 times 24 plus n minus 1 times negative 3. Set this equal to 78.

Step 2 — Simplify inside the brackets. 2 times 24 is 48. n minus 1 times negative 3 is negative 3n plus 3. So inside the brackets we have 48 minus 3n plus 3, which equals 51 minus 3n.

Step 3 — Write the equation. n over 2 times the quantity 51 minus 3n equals 78. Multiply both sides by 2: n times the quantity 51 minus 3n equals 156. Expand: 51n minus 3n squared equals 156.

Step 4 — Rearrange into standard form. 3n squared minus 51n plus 156 equals 0. Divide everything by 3: n squared minus 17n plus 52 equals 0.

Step 5 — Factorise. We need two numbers that multiply to 52 and add to negative 17. Those are negative 4 and negative 13. So the equation factors as n minus 4 times n minus 13 equals 0, giving n equals 4 or n equals 13.

Step 6 — Verify both answers. For n equals 4: the terms are 24, 21, 18, 15. Their sum is 78. Correct. For n equals 13: the 5th term onward continues 12, 9, 6, 3, 0, negative 3, negative 6, negative 9, negative 12. The terms after the 4th are positive at first, then zero, then negative. The negative terms cancel the extra positive amount, bringing the running sum back down to 78 at the 13th term.

Both solutions are valid because the common difference is negative, so terms eventually become negative and pull the sum back to 78 a second time.

Step 1: Identify the AP. The first term a is 200 and the common difference d is 10. We want the sum of the first 12 terms, so n equals 12.

Step 2: Use the sum formula — sum equals n over 2 times the quantity two times a plus n minus one times d.

Step 3: Substitute the values — sum equals 12 over 2 times the quantity two times 200 plus 11 times 10.

Step 4: Simplify inside the brackets first — two times 200 is 400, and 11 times 10 is 110, so the bracket gives 400 plus 110, which is 510.

Step 5: Multiply — 12 over 2 is 6, and 6 times 510 equals 3060.

The worker earns a total of 3060 rupees over 12 days.

questions.q_text: In an arithmetic progression, the 5th term is 23 and the common difference is 4. Find the first term and then calculate the sum of the first 10 terms.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Use the nth term formula to find the first term. The nth term equals a plus n minus one times d. For the 5th term: 23 equals a plus 4 times 4, which means 23 equals a plus 16, so a equals 7.

Step 2: Now use the sum formula to find the sum of the first 10 terms. Sum equals n over 2 times the quantity two times a plus n minus one times d, with n equal to 10, a equal to 7, and d equal to 4.

Step 3: Substitute — sum equals 10 over 2 times the quantity two times 7 plus 9 times 4.

Step 4: Simplify inside the brackets — two times 7 is 14, and 9 times 4 is 36, giving 14 plus 36 which is 50.

Step 5: Multiply — 10 over 2 is 5, and 5 times 50 equals 250.

The first term is 7 and the sum of the first 10 terms is 250.
